glance: 29 km to Narayanganj by road, 1–2 hours by bus or car
kadam-rasul-dargah.desc: On the east bank of the Shitalakshya, at Nabiganj in Bandar, a small single-domed shrine keeps a stone said to carry the footprint of the Prophet Muhammad. The Mughal chronicler Mirza Nathan wrote that the Afghan chief Masum Khan Kabuli bought the relic from merchants who had brought it from Arabia. The present shrine was built in 1777–78 by Ghulam Nabi, a Dhaka landlord, and the relic is kept in a metal dish of rose water. Many people visit on Fridays and religious days.
blocks: How to get there
From Narayanganj town cross the Shitalakshya by boat from the Bandar/Nabiganj ghat, then walk or take a rickshaw to the dargah.
Good to know
Dress modestly and remove shoes. Fridays and religious holidays are crowded.

goaldi-mosque.desc: Built in 1519 during the reign of Sultan Alauddin Husain Shah, Goaldi Mosque is one of the few surviving buildings from Sonargaon's time as a Sultanate capital. The single dome sits on a square brick hall, and the mihrabs carry delicate stone and terracotta carving. It stands in a village a short ride from Panam, and few visitors make the detour. Nearby is a later Mughal mosque, making a neat pair.
blocks: How to get there
Rickshaw or auto from Panam Nagar, about 10 minutes.
Good to know
It is still used for prayer; visit outside prayer times and dress modestly.

jamdani-weaving.desc: Jamdani is a fine cotton cloth in which motifs are woven into the fabric by hand on a pit loom, not printed or embroidered. It descends from the famous Dhaka muslin, and UNESCO recognised the art of Jamdani weaving in 2013. Two weavers sit side by side and insert each pattern thread with a bamboo stick, so a good sari can take weeks or months. Villages in Rupganj and Sonargaon upazilas, around Tarabo and Noapara, still weave in family workshops.
blocks: Good to know
Ask a local guide to arrange a visit to a weaving household; buy from weavers to support the craft.

panam-nagar.desc: Panam was a prosperous trading street of Hindu cloth merchants, and its two rows of brick mansions date mostly from the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The houses mix European columns and arches with Mughal and local details, and many still show traces of coloured glass and stucco. Most were abandoned after Partition and now stand empty along a narrow road with canals behind. Walk slowly and look up at the facades, especially in soft morning light.
blocks: How to get there
Bus from Dhaka (Gulistan) to Mograpara on the Dhaka–Chattogram highway, then a rickshaw or auto to Panam, about 1.5 hours in total.
Good to know
Combine with the Folk Arts museum nearby. Do not enter fenced, unstable buildings.

fath-shah-mosque-mograpara.desc: In Nagar Sadipur village of Mograpara, part of medieval Sonargaon, a one-domed mosque stands beside the tombs of Pir Manna Shah Darvesh and Shaykh Muhammad Yusuf. An Arabic inscription dates it to 1484, in the reign of Sultan Jalaluddin Fath Shah, and a Persian one records a Mughal rebuild in 1700–01, which gave it its present dome. Locals call it the Dargabari Shahi Jame Masjid. Most visitors to Sonargaon go only to Panam Nagar and the folk museum, so this stays quiet.
blocks: How to get there
From Mograpara chowrasta on the Dhaka–Chattogram highway, take a rickshaw or auto to the Dargabari in Nagar Sadipur.
Good to know
Fit it into a Sonargaon day with Panam Nagar and Goaldi Mosque. Avoid prayer times.

lokenath-ashram-barodi.desc: Lokenath Brahmachari spent his last years at Barodi and died here in 1890, on the 19th of Jaishtha. Every year on that day a huge tirodhan festival is held, with devotees coming from across Bangladesh and from India, Nepal and elsewhere, and a week-long fair fills the field in front. At the high point, devotees throw batasha sweets from the ashram roof for the crowd to catch, known as 'Hari loot'. Inside are his samadhi, a large painting of him and an old bakul tree; there are ponds dug in his lifetime and large pilgrim houses where devotees can stay free.
blocks: How to get there
Take a bus on the Dhaka–Chattogram highway to Mograpara or Sonargaon, then a CNG or auto to Barodi bazar; the ashram is at its north-west corner.
Good to know
On 19 Jaishtha (early June) the crowd runs into hundreds of thousands, so plan transport early. On ordinary days it is calm. Remove shoes in the ashram.

langalbandh.desc: Langalbandh, in Bandar upazila, sits on the banks of the Old Brahmaputra. Legend says the sage Parashuram was freed of his sins after bathing here, and every year on the Ashtami of the bright fortnight of Chaitra (March–April) Hindu devotees come in vast numbers, some from India and Nepal, for the Ashtami snan. A string of bathing ghats with names like Annapurna, Prematala and Jaykali line the river, along with temples and ashrams. Outside the festival it is a quiet riverside place.
blocks: How to get there
From Narayanganj or the Dhaka–Chattogram highway at Madanpur, take a CNG or auto to Langalbandh.
Good to know
During the Ashtami snan the crowds are enormous and a deadly stampede happened in 2015, so keep children close and avoid the busiest ghats at peak times.

langalbandh-ashtami-snan.desc: On the eighth day of the waxing moon in the Bangla month of Chaitra, Hindu pilgrims gather at Langalbandh in Bandar upazila to bathe in the Old Brahmaputra. The ritual is believed to wash away sins, and the bathing ghats along the river become packed with people over a day and a night. A fair grows up around the ghats with food stalls and religious goods. It is one of the largest Hindu gatherings in Bangladesh.
blocks: Good to know
Expect very large crowds; go early and respect the bathing areas.

sonargaon-folk-art-museum.desc: The Bangladesh Folk Arts and Crafts Foundation was set up by the painter Zainul Abedin in 1975 to preserve the country's rural crafts. Its main museum occupies the Sardar Bari, an ornate early 20th-century mansion, and a second building holds displays of boats, pottery, textiles, wood carving and metalwork. The grounds have ponds, shade trees and craft stalls where artisans sometimes work. A crafts fair is held here around January each year.
blocks: How to get there
Same route as Panam Nagar; the museum is a short walk or rickshaw ride away.
Good to know
Go in winter to catch the annual craft fair.

narayanganj-sweet-curd.desc: In Siddhirganj bazar, the Pran Ballabh sweet shop has sold doi, matha and kacha chhana since 1950. The kacha chhana is soft, barely sweetened curd cheese, eaten fresh by the spoonful. The doi is set in clay pots and is a local favourite for festivals and family visits. It is a simple taste of the district's dairy traditions.

sonakanda-fort.desc: Sonakanda is one of the river forts the Mughal governor Mir Jumla II is believed to have built around 1660–63 to guard Dhaka and Narayanganj from Magh and Portuguese pirates. It stands on the east bank of the Shitalakshya in Bandar, opposite Narayanganj town. The fort has a walled enclosure with loopholed battlements and, on one side, a massive raised circular platform where cannon were mounted. Together with Hajiganj and Idrakpur it forms a set of three Mughal water forts you can visit in a day.
blocks: How to get there
Cross the Shitalakshya from Narayanganj's Bandar ghat by boat or ferry, or go by road over the bridge, then take a rickshaw to Sonakanda.
Good to know
Combine it with Hajiganj Fort on the opposite bank. Mornings are quieter.

glance: 29 km to Narayanganj by road, 1–2 hours by bus or car
hajiganj-fort.desc: In the 17th century the Mughals built a chain of river forts to stop Magh and Portuguese pirates sailing up to Dhaka. Hajiganj Fort, inside Narayanganj city, is one of them: a walled enclosure with crenellated brick ramparts and a round bastion for cannon. It is small and can be seen in half an hour, but standing on the walls helps you imagine the river wars of Mughal Bengal. Sonakanda Fort, a sister fort, lies across the river at Bandar.
blocks: How to get there
Rickshaw from Narayanganj city centre (Chashara) towards Hajiganj.
Good to know
Cross by ferry to Bandar to see Sonakanda Fort as well.
